newsitem.title: UK: IEA sees sharp oil demand rise met by extra supply.
newsitem.headline: IEA sees sharp oil demand rise met by extra supply.

text.p: World oil demand will jump sharply this winter but extra supplies from new non-OPEC developments, delayed from earlier this year, will help meet the rise in consumption, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Friday.

Global demand will rise to 73.8 million barrels per day (bpd) in the fourth quarter 1996, a 100,000 bpd upward revision and up 1.9 million from the same period last year, the Paris-based agency said in its monthly oil market report.

Demand is expected to hit 74.7 million bpd in the first quarter of next year and average 73.7 million for 1997, a 1.9 million rise on the year, and a 100,000 bpd upward revision from last month's report, the IEA said.

Rising winter demand will increase the call on OPEC crude supplies plus stocks to 26 million bpd in the fourth quarter and 26.5 million in the first quarter 1997, the agency said, making minor adjustments to last month's report.

"The call on OPEC crude plus stock change for winter 1996/97 is little changed, with a 100,000 bpd (fourth quarter) increase more than offset by a 200,000 bpd (first quarter 1997) reduction," the IEA said.
The call on OPEC and stocks in the third quarter of this year was 400,000 bpd higher than expected because demand proved stronger and non-OPEC supply weaker than projected.
The agency made a 300,000 bpd retrospective downward revision to its non-OPEC supply estimate for the period and raised its assessment of world demand by 200,000 bpd.
On the supply side, the agency said world oil production hit a new record 72.9 million bpd in October, up a steep 900,000 bpd from September.
World supplies have risen from 69.88 million bpd on average last year.
OPEC output crept up in October by 90,000 bpd, topping 26 million bpd for the first time since 1980, the IEA estimated.
The agency said some of the delayed new non-OPEC supply projects now were starting to come onstream.
It said last month's report overestimated non-OPEC supply growth of 900,000 bpd in September by about 450,000 bpd.

"Despite the downward revisions to supply in September, the expected fourth quarter 1996 supply increase appears to have begun in October with several new field start-ups and seasonal upturns in existing fields in North America and the North Sea," the IEA said.
"There is some evidence that the period of downward revisions may be coming to an end."
The IEA's projections make gloomy reading for OPEC once winter has ended.
It sees the call on OPEC crude and stocks falling next year to 25.3 million bpd on average compared to 25.5 million in 1996.
